title: Digital Signature — Full Detail Knowledge Graph
topic: Digital signatures as a public-key cryptographic primitive and the surrounding security, key-management, implementation, standards, and legal ecosystem

source_policy.caveats: Claims explicitly marked as citation-needed, failed verification, or unsourced in the supplied article are represented with caveats rather than treated as independently verified.

entities.name: Digital signature
entities.description: Mathematical scheme used to verify authenticity of digital messages or documents; binds a signature to message bits and is designed to make forgery computationally infeasible.

entities.name: Electronic signature
entities.description: Electronic data carrying the intent of a signature; broader than digital signatures and does not necessarily use cryptography.

entities.name: Public-key cryptography
entities.description: Cryptographic paradigm using related public and private keys; digital signatures use the private key to sign and public key to verify.

entities.name: Private signing key
entities.description: Secret key used by a signing algorithm; disclosure permits an attacker to produce signatures attributable to the key holder.

entities.name: Public verification key
entities.description: Public key used to verify signatures; its association with an identity must itself be authenticated.

entities.name: Key generation algorithm
entities.description: Generates a private key and corresponding public key; the source formalizes this as G.

entities.name: Signing algorithm
entities.description: Takes a message and private key and outputs a signature/tag; formalized as S.

entities.name: Verification algorithm
entities.description: Takes a message, public key and signature/tag and returns accept or reject; formalized as V.

entities.name: Message / bitstring
entities.description: Arbitrary bitstring or document to be signed; signatures bind to exact signed content.

entities.name: Signature value / tag
entities.description: Cryptographic output produced by signing; it is verified against the message and public key.

entities.name: Message digest
entities.description: Short digest computed from a message by a hash function, commonly signed instead of the entire document.

entities.name: Cryptographic hash function
entities.description: Maps a message to a digest; used for efficiency and to normalize message data for signature schemes.

entities.name: Signature correctness
entities.description: A signature produced using a private key is accepted by verification with the corresponding public key.

entities.name: EUF-CMA
entities.description: Existential unforgeability under chosen-message attack: an adversary with access to signing queries should not be able to produce a valid signature on a message not queried.

entities.name: Security parameter n
entities.description: Parameter controlling the computational security scale in the formal definition; represented as unary input 1^n.

entities.name: Probabilistic polynomial time
entities.description: Formal computational model used to describe key generation, signing, verification and efficient adversaries.

entities.name: Signing oracle
entities.description: Oracle that returns signatures for adversary-selected messages in the adaptive chosen-message attack model.

entities.name: Signing query set Q
entities.description: Set of messages queried to the signing oracle; a successful EUF-CMA forgery must target a message outside this set.

entities.name: Authentication
entities.description: Evidence that a message was produced by an entity controlling the private key associated with a trusted public key.

entities.name: Integrity
entities.description: Ability to detect changes to signed message content because verification fails when signed bits are altered.

entities.name: Non-repudiation of origin
entities.description: Property intended to make it difficult for a signer to deny having signed information; depends on key custody, attribution, revocation and legal context.

entities.name: Confidentiality
entities.description: Protection of message contents from disclosure; signatures do not themselves provide confidentiality.

entities.name: Message authentication code (MAC)
entities.description: Authentication mechanism that provides confidence to a specific recipient or set of key holders, unlike public verifiability of digital signatures.

entities.name: Encryption
entities.description: Transforms plaintext to ciphertext to conceal content; by itself it does not necessarily authenticate sender or detect all unauthorized modifications.

entities.name: Public key infrastructure (PKI)
entities.description: Systems and governance used to associate public keys with identities, commonly through certificates and certificate authorities.

entities.name: Public key certificate
entities.description: Cryptographically protected record binding a public key to an identity or subject.

entities.name: Certificate authority (CA)
entities.description: PKI operator that attests to a public-key/identity association.

entities.name: Certificate revocation list (CRL)
entities.description: Published list used to check whether certificates have been revoked.

entities.name: Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP)
entities.description: Online mechanism for checking certificate status/revocation.

entities.name: Key or certificate revocation
entities.description: Process for marking a key/certificate as no longer trusted, important after compromise or loss.

entities.name: Replay attack
entities.description: Reuses a previously valid signed message to trigger an action again; signatures alone do not prevent replay.

entities.name: Transaction identifier / nonce
entities.description: Unique transaction context used to detect duplicate operations and prevent replay of signed commands.

entities.name: Signature malleability
entities.description: Ability in some schemes to transform a valid signature into another valid signature for the same message without the private key.

entities.name: Public-key authentication
entities.description: Process of verifying that a public key really belongs to the claimed signer; a signature alone does not establish this binding.

entities.name: WYSIWYS (What You See Is What You Sign)
entities.description: Requirement that the semantic content shown to the signer corresponds to the exact content actually signed, without hidden or substituted content.

entities.name: Trusted signing application
entities.description: Application whose integrity and communication with signing software are verified to prevent substitution of what is shown and what is signed.

entities.name: Smart card
entities.description: Tamper-resistant device that can hold a private key and perform signing operations without routinely exporting the key.

entities.name: Smart-card reader
entities.description: Interface used to communicate with a smart card; a separate keypad can reduce exposure of PINs to compromised host computers.

entities.name: Personal identification number (PIN)
entities.description: Code used to activate a smart card; security depends partly on PIN strength and protection.

entities.name: Hardware security module (HSM)
entities.description: Dedicated hardware used to protect cryptographic keys and perform operations, including network-attached signing services.

entities.name: Network-attached HSM
entities.description: HSM reachable over a network for centralized signing operations; introduces deployment and trust-boundary considerations.

entities.name: FIPS 201

entities.name: Document provenance

entities.name: Software distribution signing

entities.name: Financial transaction

entities.name: Contract management software

entities.name: Electronic academic transcript
entities.description: Electronic student record that can be digitally signed to help assure authenticity.

architecture_patterns.name: Sign–Verify Lifecycle
architecture_patterns.description: Canonical public-key signature lifecycle from key generation through message signing and recipient verification.
controls: Validate signer-to-key binding
Reject if verification fails
Protect private key
Apply algorithm-specific encoding and parameters

architecture_patterns.name: PKI Identity Binding and Revocation
architecture_patterns.description: Establishes trust in the public key and checks current certificate status before relying on a signature.
controls: Do not infer key identity from signature alone
Check revocation status where required
Consider CA mis-issuance and PKI governance

architecture_patterns.name: Hash-Then-Sign
architecture_patterns.description: Hash the message, encode the digest according to the signature scheme, then sign the encoded digest.
controls: Never use raw RSA signing as described
Use suitable scheme-specific encoding
Hash the exact bytes whose semantics are intended to be signed

architecture_patterns.name: Hardware-Protected Signing Key
architecture_patterns.description: Keep signing key within a smart card or HSM and authorize signing requests through protected interfaces.
controls: Keep private key non-exportable where supported
Protect PIN entry against keylogging
Authenticate calling applications
Plan revocation after loss or theft

architecture_patterns.name: WYSIWYS Trusted Presentation
architecture_patterns.description: Ensures the user-facing semantic document corresponds to the exact bitstring presented to the signing operation.
controls: Prevent hidden content and semantic substitution
Ensure displayed and signed content match
Use integrity-checked applications

architecture_patterns.name: Replay-Safe Signed Transaction
architecture_patterns.description: Combines signature verification with application-level freshness and duplicate detection.
controls: Do not use signature bytes alone as transaction IDs
Bind transaction context, audience and freshness
Reject previously processed identifiers

architecture_patterns.name: Separate Signing and Encryption Keys
architecture_patterns.description: Uses distinct key pairs for legal assent/authentication and confidentiality so encrypted communication does not automatically imply a signed agreement.
controls: Never treat encryption as legal signature by itself
Use distinct lifecycle and recovery policies
Protect signing-key backups exceptionally carefully

derived_rules.rule: A signing private key must remain secret; anyone who obtains it can generate valid signatures.
Verify the signature against the exact received message bytes; any mutation should cause rejection under a correct scheme.
A valid signature proves control of a private key only relative to a trusted binding between that public key and the claimed identity.
A signature alone does not prevent replay; add transaction identifiers, freshness checks, and duplicate detection to state-changing protocols.
Do not assume signature bytes uniquely identify a signed message or transaction; account for randomized signatures and malleability.
Ensure the content the user sees and approves is the content actually signed; protect rendering and signing applications against substitution.
Check certificate/key status where the trust model requires it, especially after loss or suspected compromise.
Do not use raw/plain RSA as a signature construction; use a secure, scheme-appropriate hash-and-encoding construction.
Use separate key pairs for signing and encryption when the application needs to distinguish assent from confidentiality.
Hardware key storage reduces exposure but does not remove PIN, reader, application, provisioning, revocation, or user-interface risks.
Do not treat non-repudiation as an automatic mathematical or legal guarantee; key custody, identity binding, revocation timing, and jurisdiction matter.
Security requires a sound algorithm, correct implementation, correct protocol use, private-key secrecy, and trusted public-key ownership binding.
Do not assume signing hides a message or that encryption alone proves authenticity; combine mechanisms according to the required security goals.

examples.name: Alice signs Hello Bob
examples.scenario: Alice signs the bitstring Hello Bob with her private key; Bob receives message and signature and verifies with Alice's trusted public key.
flow: Bob validates Alice's public-key identity binding
Bob verifies signature and rejects if message was altered
examples.lesson: Verification checks integrity and possession of the corresponding private key, assuming the public key is correctly associated with Alice.

examples.name: Signed bank transfer and replay
examples.scenario: A branch signs a transfer request. An attacker replays the same valid request if the bank lacks transaction IDs or duplicate detection.
flow: Attacker resends the same signed request
Without replay controls the transfer may execute again
Transaction ID and replay cache reject duplicate
examples.lesson: Authentication and integrity do not provide freshness or exactly-once execution by themselves.

examples.name: Authenticating a software update
examples.scenario: Publisher distributes a non-secret patch; client verifies its signature before applying it to reduce risk of malicious substitution.
flow: Client verifies signature and trusted publisher key
examples.lesson: A signature can authenticate public software artifacts even when confidentiality is unnecessary.

examples.name: Smart-card digest signing
examples.scenario: The application hashes a document and sends the digest to a smart card; the card signs using its stored private key and returns the signature.
flow: Signature is returned without exporting the private key
examples.lesson: Hardware protection reduces key-extraction risk but does not by itself guarantee correct document presentation or safe host software.

examples.name: Contract signing separate from encrypted negotiation
examples.scenario: Parties exchange confidential negotiation messages using encryption keys and sign the final contract with separate signing keys.
flow: Each party signs the agreement with signing key
Signatures are verified against trusted identities
Compromise of one key type is handled according to its separate purpose
examples.lesson: Encryption of a conversation should not be confused with signing a particular contract.
